profile.purpose: Explain the differences between table salt, kosher salt and fancy finishing salts, and when each is the right one to use.
profile.thesis: All these salts are chemically almost identical sodium chloride. The real differences are crystal shape and density, which affect volume measurements, handling and texture. That is why Serious Eats recipes call for kosher salt, while table salt and finishing salts have their own appropriate uses.
key_takeaways: Table, kosher and sea salts are nearly 100% sodium chloride; additives like anti-caking agents or trace minerals don't meaningfully affect flavor once dissolved.
The key difference is crystal geometry: tiny table salt cubes pack tightly, while kosher salt's craggy flakes trap air.
A cup of table salt weighed just over 10 oz versus about 5 oz for Diamond Crystal kosher salt, so volume measures are not interchangeable.
Morton kosher salt weighs about 80% as much as table salt by volume; a conversion chart is linked in the description.
Kosher salt is recommended mainly for handling: it is easy to pinch and sprinkle evenly, while table salt slips through the fingers.
Table salt is fine if you weigh salt by mass, and it is good in baked goods and liquids where it dissolves quickly.
Fancy finishing salts are optional; their shape adds crunch and bursts of salinity, so use them to finish dishes, not to cook.
Kenji's favorite finishing salts are a flaky English sea salt and a moist, chunky French salt, and he recommends a salt cellar for easy access.

outline.title: Intro
outline.summary: Kenji introduces the topic of salt varieties and says Serious Eats usually recommends kosher salt.

outline.title: Chemical Differences
outline.summary: Covers how all salts are essentially sodium chloride, why crystal geometry is the real difference, and a scale demonstration comparing the weight of a cup of table salt and a cup of kosher salt. Also notes the difference between Diamond Crystal and Morton.

outline.title: Why Use Kosher
outline.summary: Explains that kosher salt is preferred because it is easier to pick up and sprinkle evenly than table salt.

outline.title: When to Use Table Salt
outline.summary: Table salt is fine when weighing by mass, and useful in baking and liquids where it dissolves quickly and evenly.

outline.title: When to Use Fancy Salt
outline.summary: Covers finishing salts: their origins, how shape affects texture and perception, uses for finishing bread, cookies and meat, Kenji's favorites, and a tip to get a salt cellar.
